newsitem.title: USA: Rx for success -- Close your eyes, envision your future.
newsitem.headline: Rx for success -- Close your eyes, envision your future.

text.p: Close your eyes for a minute and imagine your future job.
What are you doing? Who is with you? What skills and resources do you need to succeed? What is your focus? What is the feeling or tone? How do you feel about yourself?
If this sounds like an exercise in idle daydreaming, it's not. Joan Goldsmith, a management expert who employs it, calls it "Vision."

"Many people may have a personal goal of moving up the ladder but unfortunately they do not have a vision for how they can transform their own lives and how they can transform the company so that it is more humane and successful," she said.
"Envisioning is a powerful technique for guiding organisations and individuals toward positive change" -- making the company "more humane and more successful."

Back in 1971, Goldsmith dreamed of creating a college for adults who had to work days, so she did. Today, 1,600 students are earning degrees nights and weekends at Cambridge College, in Cambridge, Mass., as a result of her vision.
Currently, she consults from Santa Monica, Calif., for Fortune 500 firms, some of whose managers, she says, got promoted for the wrong reasons and are holding back corporate creativity.

"They got to their positions because they were successful in the doingness of the job, the day-to-day activities, pushing the paper, writing the memos, toeing the company line, and often not even for the results they produced." The vision factor apparently played little or no role in their career climb.

Yet "visions help establish a basis of consensus within which everyone can belong," she writes in her new book, "Thank God It's Monday!" (Irwin) co-authored with Kenneth Cloke, an authority on conflict resolution.

Visions "create a sense of ownership, build teamwork and improve our communication and relationships. They allow us to begin with what we agree on so our disagreements can be put in persepctive," they write.

"How many of you have sat down with your co-workers to create a vision for how your future workplace might be organised? Have you stopped to consider all the possible ways of organising your work before you begin to reengineer your work processes?," they write.

One executive who has done just that is Jerry Scro, chief financial officer in the New York office of Showtime, the cable programming service. "I spent a lot of time on trains and planes thinking in terms of the vision of the organisation," he said.
Afterward, Scro and his 90 financial department aides held "regular sessions" of two to six days with Goldsmith and Cloke about "intensive team training and conflict resolution."

"It's been a living, breathing experience," Scro said, "and what it came down to was making it clear to people up front what was expected of them, giving them the tools to do their job, and perfomance measures they could be measured against. We're still going through the transition."

For Disney Feature Animation in Burbank, Calif., Goldsmith's task was to create "a culture of inclusion" for the technical staff "aligned with the vision created by the leaders but having meaning for them in their own work."

Disney Feature Animation President Peter Schneider wanted them to know that "the leadership group was listening to them and interested in what they had to say about where they should go," Goldsmith said.

"Customer service, strategic planning, rapidity, and flexibility cannot be maximized without a vision of the purposes and direction of the organisation to which everyone is genuinely committed," Goldsmith and Cloke believe.

A good vision statement, Goldsmith said, is not only best when it's "a little cloudy and grand" but also when it "engages our hearts and spirits," "taps into embedded concerns and needs," and "is an assertion of what we and our colleagues want to create."
(EDITORS: Sherwood Ross is a freelance writer who covers workplace issues for Reuters. Any opinions in the column are solely those of Mr. Ross.)
